content:
Bloomberg yesterday published a report stating that Apple is about to launch a brand-new "Apple Upgrade" leasing contract to replace the existing iPhone Upgrade Program.

There appear to be two major differences between the two, and one of them could be quite concerning...

The iPhone Upgrade Program operates in a fairly straightforward manner. The purchase price is spread over 24 monthly instalments, and once the two-year term ends, the device becomes entirely the property of the user, with no credit charges whatsoever.

(Additionally, users may choose to upgrade to a new iPhone after the 12th month. At that point, a new two-year contract begins, effectively meaning the old device is sold back to Apple for the amount already paid.)

Apple has yet to make any official announcement regarding the new plan, so the exact way it will operate remains unconfirmed. However, Bloomberg reports that the new plan will cover most other Apple products, with a three-year lease term for Mac. At first glance, everything seems fairly reasonable.

What is troubling, however, is that the report suggests the new plan will operate in a manner similar to car leasing. Under this type of contract, users do not gradually pay off the full price of the product over the lease term; instead, monthly payments cover only the product's depreciation during the lease period, plus any interest. When the lease term ends, users do not own the product — they have essentially been renting it all along.

Similarly, assuming the operation works like car leasing, users would need to return the product at the end of the lease term, or pay a "balloon payment" to cover the difference between the depreciation amount and the product's original price.

Of course, this means monthly payments would be lower than under the current plan. One could argue this is a good thing, as it would make Apple products more affordable for more people.

However, it is worth noting that most people do not set aside extra savings each month to prepare for that large balloon payment at the end of the lease term. The most common scenario with car leasing is that users return the car when the term expires, then sign a new lease for a new car. In other words, they become trapped in a never-ending cycle, never truly owning the product.

If the new Apple Upgrade plan operates in the same way, the situation will be identical. Users would no longer be able to choose to keep their existing phone for many years, but would instead essentially be forced to upgrade their iPhone every two years, or their Mac every three years. Even without any interest expenses, the total cost of ownership would still increase significantly in the long run.

Furthermore, if the report is accurate and the plan does not include AppleCare+, users could find themselves in a difficult situation if their device is lost, stolen, or severely damaged beyond repair during the lease term. They would not only have to continue paying monthly instalments for a device they no longer have, but would also have to pay the balloon payment at the end of the lease term.

I understand that Apple wishes to streamline operations by consolidating everything under a single upgrade plan, thereby discontinuing the current programme. But I believe that for consumers, a better approach would be to offer plans that allow users to choose for themselves — enjoying credit arrangements while maintaining control over their own upgrade cycle.

What are your thoughts on this? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
